exercises.passage:
The First Step In

A first internship can feel disappointingly ordinary: answering emails, organizing files, and watching experienced colleagues do the interesting work. Yet these small tasks serve a purpose. They teach the unspoken rules of professional life — how meetings run, how deadlines are tracked, and how colleagues ask for help — that no classroom fully explains.

The difference between a useful internship and a wasted summer is usually mentoring. Interns who meet weekly with a supervisor to review progress learn far more than those left alone with repetitive tasks. A good mentor explains not just what to do but why it matters to the team.

Pay remains controversial. Unpaid positions exclude students who cannot afford to work for free, while paid programs attract stronger applicants and treat interns as real contributors. Whatever the salary, the true test of an internship is simple: does the intern leave with skills and contacts they did not have before?
